name: 10-methods-comparison
title: Methods comparison — how every simulation method stacks up on speed and fidelity

parent_studies.rationale: Pulls the per-engine runtimes and the surrogate admissibility check into one cross-method frontier.
Pulls the per-observable fidelity numbers into one matrix across methods.
Places the radical mean-hemodynamics reduction on the shared frontier.
Places the event-driven hybrid on the frontier and grades its reproduction + admissibility.

question:
The investigation now runs the one sepsis model under many simulation methods — exact
engines, a reduced model, a learned surrogate, and the event-driven hybrid. How do they
actually stack up against each other in runtime and in results, and can we grade the
comparison rather than just assert it?
objective:
Put every method on one speed-vs-fidelity frontier from the committed run data, show the
per-observable detail (where each agrees and diverges), and grade the comparison with a
report-card Test: the exact engines agree, the hybrid reproduces them AND stays physically
admissible (the discriminating control the surrogate fails), at a competitive runtime.
claim:
The simulation methods form a clean speed-fidelity frontier, and the comparison is graded,
not asserted. The exact engines (BioGears C++, Tellurium, COPASI) are the slow faithful
reference — two independent exact-SBML integrators agree to ~5e-4. The event-free proto_valve
and the event-driven hybrid sit at the sweet spot: ~1e-3 hemodynamic error at ~1.2x the full
model's speed (233 s vs 284 s for a 2 h severe run), the hybrid adding explicit, swappable
events. The mean-hemodynamics reduction (~5.6e7x) and the PyTorch surrogate (~4e4x) buy orders
of magnitude of speed but give up fidelity — and the surrogate is inadmissible, leaving
physical bounds on 8 of 9 severe observables. A report-card Test grades this: cross-engine
agreement and hybrid hemodynamic fidelity are hard gates (both pass), physical admissibility
is a hard gate the hybrid passes and the surrogate fails (the discriminating control), runtime
is a directional axis (1.22x), and the hybrid's ~20% blood-pathogen transient is recorded as
the stated cost of the tick-quantized infection timing. The per-observable matrix localizes
every method's cost: proto_valve and the hybrid are identical everywhere except blood pathogen,
where the hybrid pays the event-relocation timing residual.

expected_behavior.name: methods-form-a-graded-speed-fidelity-frontier
expected_behavior.statement: Across methods, higher speed trades against fidelity along a clear frontier; the exact engines agree to ~1e-3, the hybrid reproduces them, and the surrogate is inadmissible — and these are graded report-card checks, not assertions.

expected_behavior.name: admissibility-discriminates-correct-from-degenerate
expected_behavior.statement: A physical-admissibility gate passes for the exact/hybrid methods and fails for the surrogate (8/9 observables out of bounds) — a discriminating control, not a trivially-wide band.

findings.summary: Every method placed on one speed-vs-fidelity frontier: exact engines (~1x, <1%), proto_valve/hybrid (~1.2x, ~1e-3), reduced (~5.6e7x, ~10%), surrogate (~4e4x, inadmissible) — chart 01.
findings.detail:
One frontier, from the committed run data (chart 01). The exact engines cluster at ~1x
speed and sub-1% error: Tellurium (reference), COPASI (~5e-4 vs Tellurium, 4.67x the raw
2 h cost), the viva-core Rust backend (bit-close, 1.12x framework), BioGears the physiology
reference. proto_valve and the event-driven hybrid sit just above 1x speed inside the
exact-fidelity band (~1e-3 hemodynamic error, 233-236 s vs 284 s for a 2 h severe run). The
mean-hemodynamics reduction (~5.6e7x) and the PyTorch surrogate (~4e4x) sit far right at
high error, the surrogate in the inadmissible zone. The per-observable matrix (chart 02)
localizes each cost: COPASI agrees everywhere (<5e-4); proto_valve and the hybrid are
identical on every observable (~6% on CO/SVR from the dropped per-beat layer, else <1%)
EXCEPT blood pathogen — exact for proto_valve (events in SBML, exact timing) but a ~20%
transient for the hybrid (events in the composition layer, seeded at the 10 s tick).
findings.statement: The comparison is a graded, admissibility-controlled frontier, not a table of assertions. Each method's cost is localized to specific observables, and the grading gate discriminates a faithful method from a degenerate one.
findings.explanation: Running one model under many methods only means something if the comparison is graded and the grade discriminates. This study does both. The speed axis is measured (same-harness 2 h runtime for the composite set; committed 48 h and per-step figures for the accelerated tiers), and the fidelity axis is the max relative error vs the appropriate exact reference, per observable. That turns the frontier into a report-card Test (methods_comparison) whose hard gates are cross-engine agreement and hybrid hemodynamic fidelity (both within_tol), whose discriminating control is physical admissibility — the exact/hybrid methods stay in bounds, the surrogate leaves 8 of 9, so the gate is not a trivially-wide band a wrong model would also pass — and whose directional axis is runtime. The per-observable matrix is the honest part: it shows proto_valve and the hybrid are the SAME continuous core (identical CO/SVR cost) and that the hybrid's only extra cost is the blood-pathogen timing transient, recorded as a soft axis rather than hidden. The placement: the exact engines are the reference where fidelity must be exact; proto_valve and the hybrid are the practical sweet spot (exact-engine fidelity, fastest-exact runtime, and for the hybrid, explicit events); the reduction and the surrogate are screening tiers whose speed is only useful inside the regime where they stay admissible — which, for the surrogate on severe sepsis, they do not.
